title: The character I almost overlooked was not a king, not a headline preacher, not a man standing on a platform with his name in lights.
paragraphs: The character I almost overlooked was not a king, not a headline preacher, not a man standing on a platform with his name in lights.
It was Epaphras.
And that should wake all of us up.

Because some of the strongest leaders in the Kingdom are not always the loudest voices in the room. Some are hidden. Some are forgotten. Some are carrying whole communities before God in prayer while nobody applauds them.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
Heaven does not measure influence the way earth does.
Paul called Epaphras “a faithful minister of Christ” and “our dear fellow servant” (Colossians 1:7). Read that again. Faithful. Dear. Fellow servant. Not flashy. Not self-promoting. Faithful.
And then the veil pulls back even more.
In Colossians 4:12, Paul writes of Epaphras, “always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.”

Always.
Labouring.
Fervently.
In prayers.
That is not passive. That is war.

Epaphras was not weak because he was hidden. He was powerful because he knew where the real battle was being fought. While others may have seen meetings, messages, and movement, Epaphras saw souls, deception, pressure, and the need for believers to stand complete in the will of God.
This is where many people miss it.

We celebrate public gifting, but often overlook private intercession. We admire the sermon, but forget the prayer that carried it. We notice the visible leader, but not the broken, surrendered servant on his knees.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior, this reminder is for the ones who feel unseen: your labor in prayer is not small. It is not secondary. It is not wasted.
But the story does not stop at leadership.
Because hidden intercession means nothing without the One being sought.

And here is the deeper issue: the reason people drift, collapse, compromise, and live powerless is not merely because they lack discipline. It is because sin has broken humanity at the root. Scripture says, “For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). We do not need better self-help. We need rescue.
That is why Jesus Christ is everything.

The same Bible that exposes our sin also reveals our hope: “But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Jesus did not come merely to inspire us. He came to save us. He bore the punishment sinners deserved, rose again in victory, and now calls men and women everywhere to repent and believe the gospel.
So yes, honor the hidden intercessor.
But do not stop there.
Become the person who runs to Christ first.

Because the greatest prayer warrior is still a sinner in need of grace. The strongest hidden leader still needs the blood of Jesus. And the one praying for others must also personally surrender to the Savior.

“For by grace are ye saved through faith… not of works, lest any man should boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9). Not by visibility. Not by reputation. Not by religious effort. By grace. Through faith. In Christ alone.
If this found you, it’s not by accident.

Maybe you thought your hidden labor did not matter. Maybe you thought your secret tears, late-night prayers, and quiet faithfulness were overlooked. But God sees. And maybe, like Epaphras, your strongest leadership is happening in a place nobody else can measure.
Still, there is one question you cannot ignore:
Are you only admiring faithful servants, or have you truly come to Jesus yourself?
